tier_reason: First-party only: main.cpp times KFAST, OpenCV cv::FAST and Rosten's fast9 on one image and the Makefile gives g++ flags, but no CPU model or compiler version is stated, and the only shown run (results.jpg screenshot, Sep 2016) predates a 2019 correctness fix in the column loop.

corrections.claimed_speedup: README: 'outperforms the next-fastest implementation by 60% single-threaded or 500% multi-threaded (!) while exactly matching its output'. results.jpg is a console screenshot of the main.cpp driver (not a bar chart): KFAST 646.711 us, OpenCV 3299.35 us ('5.102x slower than KFAST'), Dr. Rosten 13750.4 us ('21.26x slower than KFAST'), all 8361 keypoints agreeing. With the driver's default KFAST_multithread = true this is multi-threaded KFAST against single-threaded OpenCV and Rosten code. No single-threaded measurement is shown for the 60% figure; the main.cpp header instead says '40-60% single-threaded or 500% multi-threaded' over 'the reference implementation'.
corrections.baseline: Edward Rosten's reference FAST-9 C code (fast9_detect / fast9_detect_nonmax in the repo's Rosten folder) and OpenCV's cv::FAST, both timed in main.cpp
corrections.workload: FAST-9 corner detection with non-maximal suppression (threshold 50) on one grayscale image (test.jpg); 150 warm-ups then the mean of 1000 timed calls per implementation, with a keypoint-equality check across all three. results.jpg is the screenshot of the output, not a test image.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Makefile: g++ (version not stated) with -Ofast -std=gnu++17 -march=native -mavx2 -mfma -flto -funroll-all-loops -fpeel-loops -ftracer -ftree-vectorize -fomit-frame-pointer; Rosten's C is built with gcc and the same flags; OpenCV is the system library (version and build flags not stated). The screenshot looks like a Windows console, so the measured build may have been MSVC; this is not stated.
corrections.caveats: The headline 5.1x ('500%') compares multi-threaded KFAST with single-threaded cv::FAST and single-threaded scalar Rosten code; the single-threaded 60% claim has no published measurement. One image, one threshold, no CPU model, no compiler version, OpenCV version unknown. The screenshot was added on Sep 12, 2016, before the Oct 2016 'horizontal AVX shuffle' performance commit and before PR #2 (Jan 2019), which fixed an off-by-one in the main column loop (j < cols - 35 instead of cols - 34) that let last_cols_mask = (1 << 32) - 1 overflow; the maintainer said this undefined shift fails to catch any corners in the last 32 columns for affected image widths. The measured image passed the driver's equality check, so the shown run was not affected. Requires AVX2 with no fallback. Last code changes 2016 to January 2019; the 2021 commit only adds the MIT LICENSE; the Rosten folder is BSD-3-Clause. It is a computer-vision kernel rather than a general SIMD library.

notes: Keep at C. The screenshot gives the real numbers: 5.102x over OpenCV and 21.26x over Rosten, both for multi-threaded KFAST against single-threaded baselines. No like-for-like single-thread figure is published. A 2019 merged fix corrected undefined-shift behaviour that dropped corners in the last 32 columns for some widths; the timed image was unaffected. One WebSearch found no independent measurement.

tier_reason: The README speedup table (39x/5.3x, 31x/3.8x, 14x/2.2x, 7.8x/1.6x) is first-party with no benchmark code in the repo (test.cpp is a correctness test only) and no CPU, compiler version, flags, sizes or mask distribution.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: README: supports clang, gcc and MSVC, and its simple correctness tests (test.cpp) were exercised on all three; no compiler versions, flags or CPU are given for the speedup table, and the repo has no benchmark code.
corrections.workload: AVX2 left-pack (compress) of one 256-bit vector per call (32 8-bit, 16 16-bit, 8 32-bit or 4 64-bit elements), driven by an integer bitmask or a vector mask; needs AVX2 plus BMI2 (PDEP/PEXT) and POPCNT, with *_Zen2 variants that avoid PDEP/PEXT for AMD Zen1/Zen2.
corrections.caveats: First-party table only. The repo holds leftpack.h and test.cpp, and test.cpp checks every mask exhaustively against the branchless scalar loop for correctness but times nothing, so the speedups cannot be reproduced from public code. No CPU, compiler, flags, input size or mask distribution are stated. The 'super naive' branchy loop mispredicts on random masks, so the 39x end flatters the result; the branchless loop (1.6x to 5.3x) is the fairer scalar baseline. The claim that it beats AVX-512 VCOMPRESS has no numbers. Every call writes a full 32 bytes at pOut whatever the kept count, so the caller must provide slack. The PDEP/PEXT versions are very slow on Zen1/Zen2. Last commit 2023-10-04, three years and one week before the run date.

notes: Numbers match the README exactly; tier C stays because no benchmark harness exists in the repo. Baseline is the scalar C++ reference loop, which is in the category's baseline list. Small, 4 stars, MIT, header-only.

tier_reason: README table names a CPU (Ryzen 9 6900HX) but the compiler is not stated, and the public benchmark/benchmark.cpp times only PTMS: the std::sort and tbb::parallel_sort rows have no public harness, so this is first-party with partial methodology.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Compiler not stated (README lists GCC 9+, Clang 10+, MSVC 2019+ via clang-cl). CMakeLists.txt defaults to a Release build and, for GCC/Clang, adds -O3 and -march=native (SIMD=AUTO) plus OpenMP with -std=c++17; MSVC gets /O2 with /arch:AVX2 or /arch:AVX512.
corrections.workload: Sorting 4,000,000 uniform random ints in [-1e6, 1e6] (fixed seed) with OpenMP tasks, parallel merging and AVX2/AVX-512 bitonic base cases; median of 600 timed runs after 400 warm-ups, with the input re-copied outside the timer before each run, at 16 threads on the 6900HX (AVX2 path, since that CPU lacks AVX-512).
corrections.caveats: The baseline rows cannot be reproduced. benchmark/benchmark.cpp times only PTMS, with no std::sort or tbb::parallel_sort code anywhere and no TBB link in CMakeLists.txt. The PTMS timer wraps ptms::detail::sort_body inside an OpenMP parallel region that is already open, with a preallocated scratch buffer, so it leaves out the parallel-region start-up the public ptms::sort_int pays on each call. The headline 18.4x compares 16 threads with one-thread std::sort; the like-for-like result is about 2.2x over tbb::parallel_sort (CITATION.cff says '~2x on cache-resident data'). The 'cache-resident' label is doubtful: the 16 MB input plus a 16 MB scratch buffer is 32 MB on a CPU with 16 MB of L3. The same input is re-sorted 1000 times. One size, int keys only, compiler unstated; the Ryzen 7 7500F AVX-512 figure (0.0162 s at 12 threads) has no baseline numbers. The repo is brand new with no external verification, and the LICENSE and CITATION.cff say 2025 (author Andrey Afimov) although the first commit is 2026-10-10. It is a parallel sort more than a SIMD library and would fit the wave-1 sorting category, where std::sort is the listed baseline.

notes: The README numbers match (0.300 / 0.036 / 0.0163 s), but only the PTMS row comes from public code; the std::sort and TBB rows have no harness, and the PTMS timer excludes OpenMP team start-up. Consider category override to sorting (with domain override); baseline_in_list would then be true.
